sub_question: What specific architecture, token economics (including the ~15x token multiplier), parallelization strategy, and evaluation results does Anthropic report for its multi-agent research system in its 2024-2025 engineering writeups, and on which task shapes does it claim multi-agent beats single-agent?
summary:
Anthropic's June 13, 2025 engineering post 'How we built our multi-agent research system' is the canonical primary source for the company's Claude Research feature. The system uses an orchestrator-worker architecture: a LeadResearcher agent (Claude Opus 4 in the headline configuration) analyzes the user query, plans an approach, persists that plan to an external Memory store (because total state can exceed Claude's 200,000-token context window and would otherwise be truncated), then spawns specialized Subagents (Claude Sonnet 4) that operate in parallel with their own context windows, prompts, and tools. Subagents perform iterative web searches, use interleaved thinking to evaluate tool results, and return condensed findings. The LeadResearcher synthesizes results and either spawns additional subagents or exits the loop; once complete, a separate CitationAgent walks the report and attaches source citations. Execution is currently synchronous (lead waits for each batch of subagents), which Anthropic flags as a bottleneck they expect to relax with async execution as models improve. An additional pattern (in the appendix) has subagents write outputs directly to a filesystem and pass lightweight references back, to avoid the 'game of telephone' fidelity loss and token blowup from copying large artifacts through the coordinator's chat history.

The headline evaluation result: a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as lead and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on Anthropic's internal research eval. The motivating example is 'identify all the board members of the companies in the Information Technology S&P 500' — the multi-agent system decomposed this into per-company subtasks, while the single agent failed because of slow, sequential searches. Anthropic explicitly attributes the gain to token-economics rather than emergent reasoning: in their analysis of the BrowseComp benchmark (which tests browsing agents on hard-to-find information), three factors explained 95% of performance variance, with token usage alone explaining 80%, and tool-call count plus model choice making up the rest. Their interpretation: multi-agent architectures are mostly a way to scale total token spend across multiple separate context windows, getting around single-agent context limits and adding parallel reasoning capacity. They also note that upgrading to Claude Sonnet 4 produced bigger gains than doubling the token budget on Claude Sonnet 3.7 — i.e., model quality is a stronger lever than raw token volume.

The token economics are blunt: Anthropic reports that 'agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats.' They state directly that 'for economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance.' Parallelization is structured around explicit scaling rules baked into prompts: simple fact-finding uses 1 agent with 3–10 tool calls; direct comparisons use 2–4 subagents with 10–15 calls each; complex research uses more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. Two layers of parallelism are exploited — the lead spins up 3–5 subagents in parallel rather than serially, and each subagent uses 3+ tools in parallel — yielding what Anthropic claims is up to a 90% reduction in research time on complex queries.

On task shape, Anthropic is explicit about wins and losses. Multi-agent wins on (1) breadth-first queries with multiple independent directions, (2) information that exceeds a single context window, (3) heavy parallelization, and (4) tasks needing many complex tools. Multi-agent loses on (1) domains where all agents must share the same context, (2) tasks with many cross-agent dependencies, and (3) most coding tasks, because they involve fewer truly parallelizable subtasks and current LLMs 'are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time.' Documented failure modes during development included subagents spawning 50 sub-subagents for simple queries, scouring the web endlessly for nonexistent sources, distracting each other with excessive updates, and duplicating work because of vague delegation (one subagent investigating the 2021 automotive chip crisis while two others independently re-investigated the 2025 supply chain). Mitigations were primarily prompt-engineering: detailed delegation contracts (objective, output format, tool/source guidance, task boundaries), embedded scaling rules, broad-to-narrow search heuristics, source-quality heuristics added after human testers caught a bias toward SEO content farms, extended-thinking 'scratchpad' planning, and a tool-testing agent that rewrote MCP tool descriptions and produced a 40% drop in task completion time. Evaluation used ~20 starting test queries, an LLM-as-judge with a single-prompt 0.0–1.0 rubric (factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, tool efficiency), plus human evaluation for edge cases. Production reliability mitigations included full tracing, resume-from-checkpoint instead of restart, and rainbow deployments to avoid breaking long-running stateful agents.

sub_question: What are the concrete arguments and failure modes (context fragmentation, handoff loss, decision dispersion, error compounding) cited in Cognition AI's 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' essay and similar 2024-2025 critiques (e.g., from LangChain, Devin postmortems), and what task shapes do they identify as losing for multi-agent designs?
summary:
Cognition AI's June 2025 essay 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' (by Walden Yan, Cognition co-founder and Devin's CPO) is the canonical critique. It frames the issue as one of *context engineering*, defined as the dynamic discipline of getting the right tokens in front of each LLM call, and argues that the dominant 'orchestrator + parallel sub-workers' pattern violates two principles so consistently that it should be ruled out by default. Principle 1: 'Share context, and share full agent traces, not just individual messages' — the original task plus every prior tool call, observation, and decision must reach each downstream agent, because in production conversations are multi-turn and any earlier detail can flip the correct interpretation of a sub-task. Principle 2: 'Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results' — even when both sub-agents see the original task, two parallel writers will make uncoordinated implicit choices (visual style, code patterns, edge-case handling) that the final aggregator cannot reconcile. The illustrative Flappy Bird example: one sub-agent silently builds a Super Mario-style background while another builds a bird with the wrong physics, and the combiner is stuck with two miscommunications.

From these principles Cognition derives concrete failure modes: (a) context fragmentation — subagents work from a sliver of the trace and misinterpret intent; (b) decision dispersion — parallel writers make conflicting implicit decisions because 'context isn't able to be shared thoroughly enough between the agents'; (c) handoff loss / compression at boundaries — even when the original prompt is forwarded, the multi-turn history and tool-call rationale get dropped; (d) error compounding over long horizons, which is what makes reliability collapse on long tasks; and (e) inability of today's agents to engage in the 'long-context proactive discourse' that would let them resolve conflicts the way human engineers do. The recommended default is a single-threaded linear agent, optionally augmented by a *separate compressor model* that distills history into key events/decisions when the context window overflows. Architectures Cognition explicitly rules out as 'fragile' include: orchestrator + parallel writer subagents, agent-to-agent debate/negotiation swarms (à la AutoGen, OpenAI Swarm), and edit-apply two-model pipelines where a small model interprets a large model's markdown diff (cited as a 2024-era Devin pattern that proved unreliable due to instruction ambiguity).

Task shapes Cognition identifies as losing for multi-agent: write-heavy tasks where outputs must be stylistically and semantically consistent (cloning a game, building a coherent codebase, refactors), tasks requiring 'human taste and decision-making', and any long-running task whose success criteria aren't simply verifiable. Task shapes that survive: read-only sub-tasks (web search, code search, Devin's Deepwiki call-out), where contradictions in retrieved info are tolerable, and which the essay characterizes as 'mostly resemble tool calls rather than true multi-agent collaboration.' Claude Code's June 2025 design is held up as the worked example: it spawns subtask agents but never runs writers in parallel and confines subagents to investigative Q&A, deliberately trading parallelism for reliability.

Independent 2024-2025 critiques converge on the same diagnosis from different angles. All Hands AI's 'Don't Sleep on Single-Agent Systems' (Graham Neubig, Sept 2024, framed around OpenHands/CodeActAgent) argues that a strong general LLM + a general action space (write code, run code, browse) + a single prompting technique can subsume most multi-agent setups, and that multi-agent difficulties 'map onto human organizational' pathologies — bad communication, skill loss when a member leaves. LangChain's 'How to think about agent frameworks' (Harrison Chase, April 2025) does not attack multi-agent per se but pins reliability failures on the same root cause: 'the hard part of building reliable agentic systems is making sure the LLM has the appropriate context at each step', and frames multi-agent as fundamentally a communication-and-context problem ('the key part of multi-agent systems is how they communicate'). Chase further argues most production 'agentic systems' are blends of workflows and agents and that abstractions which obfuscate what context flows into the LLM at each step are anti-reliability. The Berkeley/Stanford MAST paper 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?' (arXiv 2503.13657, ICLR/NeurIPS 2025), with 1,600+ annotated traces across seven MAS frameworks, formalizes 14 failure modes in three buckets — system-design issues, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification — and the search-surfaced excerpts name conversation reset, task derailment, information withholding, and failure to ask for clarification as recurring patterns; this is corroborating empirical evidence for Cognition's qualitative claims, although I did not fetch the paper directly.

A significant nuance: Cognition itself softened in April 2026's 'Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working'. Yan now reports that *narrow* multi-agent patterns ship reliably when 'writes stay single-threaded and the additional agents contribute intelligence rather than actions.' Two work today: (1) a generator-verifier loop where Devin Review reads only the diff with a clean context and catches an average of two bugs per Devin-authored PR (~58% of them severe logic/security bugs) — counterintuitively, the reviewer performs *better* without shared context because of attention dilution / 'context rot'; and (2) a 'smart friend' delegation where a fast primary model (e.g., SWE-1.5/1.6 or a Sonnet-class) escalates to a frontier model (Opus-class, GPT) for the trickiest sub-decisions. Manager-Devin spawning child Devins via an internal MCP is in production but required substantial engineering on cross-agent communication; unstructured swarms remain 'mostly a distraction.' The two-essay arc therefore reads less as a reversal than as scoping: parallel writers that fragment decisions still lose; isolated read-only or verifier sub-agents that inject intelligence without taking conflicting write actions can win.

key_facts.claim: Cognition's 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' (June 12, 2025) names two principles whose violation rules out most multi-agent architectures: (1) share context and full agent traces, not just messages; (2) actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting parallel decisions yield bad results.

The canonical failure example is the Flappy Bird clone: parallel subagents produce a Super-Mario-styled background and a non-Flappy-Bird-styled bird, and even when the original task is shared, two parallel writers diverge on style/edge-cases because they cannot see each other's actions in real time.

Cognition argues that multi-agent fragility stems from 'decision-making ends up being too dispersed and context isn't able to be shared thoroughly enough between the agents'; today's agents cannot conduct the 'long-context proactive discourse' needed to resolve disagreements as humans do.

Cognition's recommended default is a single-threaded linear agent; for long-context overflow, introduce a dedicated compression LLM (potentially a fine-tuned small model) that distills history into key events and decisions, rather than splitting the task across parallel agents.

As of June 2025 Claude Code intentionally never runs writer subagents in parallel and confines subagents to investigative Q&A, treating them as a context-budget device, not a true delegation pattern — Cognition cites this as evidence that production designers reach the same conclusion.

Cognition explicitly cites a 2024-era 'edit-apply' Devin pattern (large model emits markdown diff → small model rewrites the file) as a real-world handoff-loss failure: the small model misinterpreted the large model's instructions on slight ambiguities, so the industry consolidated edit decisioning and applying into a single model action.

In Cognition's April 2026 follow-up, the working multi-agent patterns are: (a) a clean-context Devin Review verifier that catches ~2 bugs per Devin PR, ~58% severe (logic, edge cases, security); and (b) a 'smart friend' tool whereby a faster primary model escalates to a frontier model. The shared rule is that 'writes stay single-threaded and the additional agents contribute intelligence rather than actions.'

Cognition attributes a key reason verifier subagents work to 'Context Rot' / attention-head dilution: a reviewer with short, fresh context outperforms a coding agent burdened with the full trace because models 'make less intelligent decisions at longer and longer context lengths.'

Cognition explicitly characterizes 'unstructured-swarm' multi-agent (arbitrary agent-to-agent negotiation) as 'mostly a distraction'; the practical viable shape is map-reduce-and-manage where a manager splits, children execute, and the manager synthesizes.

All Hands AI's 'Don't Sleep on Single-Agent Systems' (Graham Neubig, Sept 26, 2024) argues that a single LLM, single (general) action space (write code, run code, browse), and single prompting technique can subsume most multi-agent designs; multi-agent issues 'map onto human organizations' (poor communication, skill loss).
All Hands concedes multi-agent is justified when one agent has privileged information or when different agents act on behalf of different principals, but treats this as exception, not default.

LangChain's Harrison Chase frames the same failure mode as 'making sure the LLM has the appropriate context at each step' being the hard part; for multi-agent, 'the key part of multi-agent systems is how they communicate', i.e., multi-agent is fundamentally a context-engineering problem.

Chase argues most production 'agentic systems' are blends of workflows and agents, and that frameworks whose abstractions obfuscate what context reaches the LLM at each step actively damage reliability — naming agent-class abstractions in early LangChain, OpenAI Agents SDK, and CrewAI as examples.

Task shapes Cognition flags as losing for multi-agent: write-heavy and stylistically-coupled tasks (game cloning, refactoring, real software requiring 'human taste'); winning shapes: read-only sub-tasks (web search, code search à la Devin's Deepwiki), generator-verifier loops on diffs, and tasks with simple verifiable success criteria (compilers, browsers, training-script optimization).

The MAST paper (Cemri et al., arXiv 2503.13657, ICLR/NeurIPS 2025) collected 1,600+ annotated traces across seven MAS frameworks and codified 14 failure modes in three categories (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification), independently corroborating Cognition's qualitative claims about coordination/handoff failure.

Cognition's June 2025 essay was published one day before Anthropic's pro-multi-agent research blog; the two pieces converged on the same first area where multi-agent works — read-only subagents — despite their opposite headline framing.

disagreements: Cognition's June 2025 essay tells readers to 'rule out by default' any architecture violating its two principles (i.e., almost all parallel-writer multi-agent), but Cognition's own April 2026 follow-up endorses certain multi-agent patterns (clean-context verifiers, smart-friend escalation, manager-with-children for scope). The two pieces are reconciled by scoping: parallel *writers* still lose; agents that contribute *intelligence* without taking conflicting actions can win.

Cognition's framing implies multi-agent for deep research is also fragile in principle, but Anthropic's contemporaneous multi-agent-research blog reports the opposite — that parallel sub-agents *do* work for breadth-first read-only research. Cognition's 2026 follow-up partially concedes this by noting that read-only subagents were the first viable area both teams converged on; the dispute is about how broadly that exception generalizes beyond research-style fan-out.

All Hands AI (Sept 2024) and LangChain (April 2025) reach Cognition-like conclusions about reliability, but their prescriptions diverge: All Hands recommends a single-action-space generalist agent (CodeActAgent style); LangChain recommends an explicit orchestration framework (LangGraph) that blends workflows and agents and exposes per-step context control. Cognition recommends single-threaded plus a custom compression LLM. None of the three has published head-to-head numbers against the others.

Search-surfaced commentary (e.g., the MongoDB and zenn.dev syntheses) frames Cognition vs Anthropic as 'saying the same thing' (memory/context engineering is the bottleneck); Cognition's primary text is more prescriptive than that synthesis suggests — Yan explicitly tells readers to 'rule out' violating architectures, not merely to engineer context more carefully.

sub_question: What head-to-head empirical results on GAIA, BrowseComp, HLE, DeepResearch Bench, or FRAMES compare single-agent vs multi-agent / orchestrator-worker LLM research systems published in 2024-2025 arXiv papers or vendor technical reports, including absolute scores, deltas, and token/latency costs?
summary:
Across the five benchmarks of interest, the picture is split by task shape and by whether token compute is held constant. On Anthropic's internal breadth-first research eval, a multi-agent orchestrator-worker (Claude Opus 4 lead + Sonnet 4 subagents) beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2%, and on BrowseComp Anthropic reports that 80% of cross-system performance variance is explained by token usage alone (with model choice and tool-call count adding ~15% more). The flip side: agents use ~4× more tokens than a chat, and the multi-agent variant uses ~15× more — Anthropic itself states multi-agent only pays off when task value justifies the budget, and that coding/tightly-coupled tasks are a poor fit. A March-2026 Anthropic follow-up reports Opus 4.6 BrowseComp at 86.81% (multi-agent, adjusted to 86.57% after removing eval-leakage cases), and finds the multi-agent configuration encounters 'unintended solutions' at 0.87% vs 0.24% for single-agent (3.7×) — a direct, undesired side effect of parallel fan-out and higher token budgets.

DeepResearch Bench (Du et al., arXiv:2506.11763, 100 PhD-level tasks, 22 fields, RACE+FACT framework) gives the cleanest production-system comparison. Orchestrator-worker 'Deep Research' products dominate single-pass LLM-with-search variants: Gemini-2.5-Pro Deep Research 48.88 RACE (111.21 effective citations), OpenAI Deep Research 46.98 (40.79 cites), Perplexity Deep Research 42.25 (31.26 cites), versus best single-agent LLM-with-search Claude-3.7-Sonnet w/Search at 40.67 (32.48 cites) and GPT-4o-Search-Preview(high) at 35.10. The lift from orchestrator-worker is ~6–8 RACE points and 2–3× more effective citations for breadth-first report-style work.

The counter-evidence comes from a Stanford budget-controlled study (Tran & Kiela, arXiv:2604.02460) on FRAMES (Krishna et al. 2025) and MuSiQue 4-hop. Holding 'thinking tokens' constant across SAS and five MAS architectures (Sequential, Subtask-parallel, Parallel-roles, Debate, Ensemble) on Qwen3-30B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Gemini-2.5-Pro, single-agent matches or exceeds the best MAS at all but the smallest (100-token) budgets. Representative numbers on Gemini-2.5-Pro FRAMES @ 5K tokens: SAS 0.700, Sequential 0.680, Debate 0.700, Ensemble 0.710, Parallel-roles 0.700; MuSiQue 4-hop @ 5K: SAS 0.419, Debate 0.470. The paper grounds this in the Data Processing Inequality — message-passing between agents can only lose information vs an unbroken context — and shows MAS only overtakes SAS when the single-agent context is corrupted (substitution α=0.7: SAS 0.200, Sequential 0.225). Their reading is that much of the apparent multi-agent gain in prior work, including Anthropic's, is unaccounted compute.

A second 2026 arXiv (Żywot et al., 2601.11327) tests small-MAS vs large-SAS on GAIA, GPQA, HLE, AIME, MuSiQue with orchestrator-only thinking: an 8B-orchestrator + 1.7B sub-agents matches a 32B direct-tools single agent on GAIA (23.0 vs 23.0), beats it on AIME (55.0 vs 45.0), trails slightly on GPQA (58.6 vs 60.1) and MuSiQue (14.0 vs 15.0), and HLE is essentially unsolved (~4%) by either. Critically, the 8B MAS runs in 7.9s/query vs 32.9s for the 32B direct (4.2× faster), and structured-memory MAS uses 9.1–11.7K tokens vs 19.5K for the SAS+thinking baseline (43% reduction). Sub-agent thinking adds 6.1s of latency for no accuracy gain — orchestrator capacity is the dominant lever, sub-agent scaling is not.

For coding/tightly-coupled work the public consensus (Cognition 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' + Anthropic's own caveat) is single-agent. For benchmark numbers, Microsoft's Magentic-One multi-agent achieves ~38% on GAIA with o1 and ~32% with GPT-4o; H2O.ai's single-agent code-first agent reports 65% on the GAIA leaderboard, beating Magentic-One's multi-agent setup using a simpler architecture and a strong code-execution tool. This corroborates the Stanford and Żywot findings: when the bottleneck is reasoning quality and tool selection rather than search breadth, a well-tooled single agent can match or beat a multi-agent stack.

Net: Anthropic's +90% gain and DeepResearch Bench's 6–8-point Deep-Research lead are real for breadth-first, citation-heavy report generation where parallel fan-out can scour many independent leads simultaneously. Stanford's SAS≥MAS finding is real for multi-hop reasoning under matched compute. Both can be true because they measure different regimes.

sub_question: How do production deep-research products (OpenAI Deep Research, Google Gemini Deep Research, Perplexity Deep Research, You.com, GPT Researcher) describe their internal architecture — single long-horizon agent vs orchestrator-worker vs planner-executor — and what published numbers exist on their cost, latency, and benchmark performance?
summary:
Production deep-research products fall into three architecturally distinct camps. (1) **Orchestrator-worker / multi-agent**: Anthropic's Claude Research is the canonical example. A LeadResearcher agent plans, saves the plan to memory (to survive the 200K-token context cap), spawns 3–5 parallel subagents with separate context windows, then hands findings to a CitationAgent for source attribution. Anthropic explicitly chose this because 'the essence of search is compression' and subagents let you parallelise it. The open-source GPT Researcher ships a similar pattern: a 'planner' agent generates research questions and 'execution' agents run searches, with a 7-agent LangGraph variant (Chief Editor, Researcher, Editor, Reviewer, Revisor, Writer, Publisher) for editorial polish. (2) **Planner-executor**: Google's Gemini Deep Research is described in its own developer docs as a Plan→Search→Read→Iterate→Output loop with optional 'collaborative planning' (the agent returns a plan first, the user edits, then the agent executes); it must run async (`background=True`) because runs span minutes. (3) **Single long-horizon agent**: OpenAI Deep Research is a single o3-based agent post-trained end-to-end with RL on real-world browsing/analysis tasks — there is no public claim of subagents. Perplexity Deep Research follows the same pattern: a single agent with a 'test-time compute expansion' loop over Perplexity's proprietary search/index (which itself is the differentiator). The Anthropic vs Cognition disagreement maps almost perfectly onto this taxonomy: Anthropic argues multi-agent is required when work is breadth-first and parallelisable; Cognition's 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' (June 2025) argues single-threaded linear agents are more reliable because subagents inevitably lose context, make conflicting implicit decisions, and produce 'telephone-game' integration failures.

On **cost**, Anthropic publishes the most concrete number: agents use ~4× the tokens of a chat turn, and multi-agent systems use ~15× — and that token spend itself accounts for 80% of BrowseComp performance variance, with token usage + tool calls + model choice explaining 95%. Anthropic also reports that switching to parallel tool calling (lead spawning 3–5 subagents concurrently, subagents calling 3+ tools concurrently) cut wall-clock research time by up to 90% on complex queries. GPT Researcher's docs put a single planner-executor run at ~3 minutes and ~$0.005–0.10 with gpt-4o-mini/gpt-4o. OpenAI Deep Research runs 5–30 minutes per query and was launched only on the $200/month Pro tier. Perplexity Deep Research is the latency leader at 2–4 minutes per query with a free tier; its underlying Perplexity Search API hits a p50 of 358 ms (vs Exa 1375 ms, Brave 513 ms).

On **benchmarks**, two cross-cutting evals dominate. On Humanity's Last Exam, OpenAI Deep Research scored 26.6% (vs 21.1% for Perplexity Deep Research, 13.0% for o3-mini-high, 9.4% for DeepSeek-R1, 6.2% for Gemini Thinking). On GAIA, OpenAI Deep Research set SOTA at 67.36% pass@1 / 72.57% cons@64 (Level 3: 47.6 / 58.03), well above the prior 63.64 average. On the academic DeepResearch Bench (100 PhD-level tasks, RACE rubric), Gemini-2.5-Pro Deep Research leads at 48.88 overall, with OpenAI Deep Research at 46.98, Perplexity Deep Research at 42.25, and Grok Deeper Search at 40.24 — but the citation profiles differ sharply: Gemini emits 111.21 effective citations per report at 81.44% accuracy, OpenAI 40.79 at 77.96%, Perplexity 31.26 at 90.24%. The ResearchRubrics paper (arXiv 2511.07685) finds that even the strongest deep-research agents stay below 68% average rubric compliance, and that no system simultaneously achieves breadth and precision. Anthropic's only public head-to-head ablation is internal: a multi-agent system using Opus 4 as lead and Sonnet 4 as subagents beat a single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research eval. Perplexity's own Search-API benchmarks (FRAMES 0.453, BrowseComp 0.371, HLE 0.288, SimpleQA 0.930) are reported only against rival search APIs (Exa, Brave, Tavily-SERP) rather than other deep-research products.

The net architectural picture: the only product publicly defending an explicit multi-agent orchestrator-worker design is Anthropic's; OpenAI and Perplexity ship single agents (their differentiation lives in the post-training and the search index, respectively); Google sits in the middle with a planner-executor loop that exposes the plan to the user. On benchmarks, the multi-agent and single-agent leaders are within ~2 RACE points of each other (Gemini 48.88 vs OpenAI 46.98), suggesting architecture alone does not determine performance — token budget, search-index quality, and model choice matter at least as much.

sub_question: What documented evidence exists that multi-agent deep-research architectures introduce or amplify specific failure modes — prompt injection / lethal-trifecta exposure via sub-agent web fetches, hallucinated handoffs, planner drift, citation fabrication — that a single-agent design avoids or mitigates, including any 2024-2025 red-team studies or postmortems?
summary:
Public 2024–2025 evidence converges on four failure modes that are either uniquely introduced by multi-agent architectures or measurably amplified by them relative to a single ReAct/CodeAct loop. (1) Hallucinated handoffs and conflicting implicit decisions are the central thesis of Cognition AI's June 2025 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' postmortem from production Devin work: their canonical Flappy Bird example shows one sub-agent rendering a Mario-style background while a parallel sub-agent builds a bird with incompatible style, because each sub-agent only sees its own slice of context. Cognition concludes that 'actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results' and recommends single-threaded linear agents by default; even forwarding the original task as context is insufficient when intermediate tool calls and multi-turn nuance also matter. They explicitly note that Claude Code's sub-agents are deliberately limited to read-only investigation, never parallel writes, for this reason.

(2) Planner drift / fanout pathology is documented inside Anthropic's own June 2025 'How we built our multi-agent research system' engineering post — the strongest pro-multi-agent source in the corpus, which still concedes that early versions of Claude Research suffered from 'spawning 50 subagents for simple queries, scouring the web endlessly for nonexistent sources, and distracting each other with excessive updates,' plus duplicated work (one subagent on the 2021 chip crisis, two others redundantly on 2025 supply chains). Anthropic's mitigations are all multi-agent-specific: scaling rules embedded in the lead-agent prompt (1 agent / 3–10 calls for fact-finding vs. >10 agents for complex research), an LLM-judge rubric, a separate CitationAgent that runs only after research closes, and a rainbow-deployment scheme. The same post quantifies the cost trade-off: agents use ~4× chat-level tokens, multi-agent systems ~15× — so the failure-mode mitigations come with an order-of-magnitude budget premium.

(3) Prompt injection / lethal-trifecta exposure is structurally amplified by sub-agent web fetches. Simon Willison's June 2025 'lethal trifecta' framing (private-data access + untrusted-content exposure + external-communication / exfiltration vector) applies to any tool-using agent, but every additional sub-agent that fetches third-party content multiplies the second leg of the trifecta. Lee & Tiwari's NeurIPS 2024 paper 'Prompt Infection: LLM-to-LLM Prompt Injection within Multi-Agent Systems' (arXiv:2410.07283) shows experimentally that injected instructions self-replicate across interconnected agents 'much like a computer virus,' propagating silently 'even when agents do not publicly share all communications,' and they propose an 'LLM Tagging' mitigation. The 2025 AgentXploit work (arXiv:2505.05849) reports 71% / 70% attack success rates on the AgentDojo and VWA-adv benchmarks against o3-mini and GPT-4o agents — roughly 100% relative improvement over those benchmarks' built-in baselines — confirming that tool-using agents remain highly compromisable. Even Anthropic's hardened browser-use Claude reports a residual ~1% attack success rate after RL training, classifiers, and intervention layers, and explicitly says 'no browser agent is immune.' A single agent with one fetch tool exposes one attack surface per turn; an orchestrator-worker fanning out N parallel web sub-agents exposes N surfaces, any one of which can poison the shared report — the same propagation pattern the Prompt Infection paper formalizes.

(4) Citation fabrication is not unique to multi-agent (Perplexity's single-pass product hallucinates citations badly per Martin Chang's February 2025 postmortem, and NYT/Chicago Tribune lawsuits in December 2025 cite trademark-attached hallucinations), but multi-agent architectures structurally aggravate it because the writing/synthesis agent often cannot see the raw retrieved text its workers saw — only their summaries. Anthropic's response is architectural: they segregate a dedicated CitationAgent that 'processes the documents and research report to identify specific locations for citations' as a separate stage, precisely to plug this gap. The June 2025 Galileo / Augment Code analyses describe the same pattern as 'lossy compression' across handoffs — short-term memory fragments across agents and edge-case details get smoothed out before the writer ever sees them. GPTZero's January 2026 audit of 4,841 NeurIPS 2025 papers, which found 100+ hallucinated citations across 51 published papers, illustrates that 'vibe citing' survives even multi-reviewer scrutiny, suggesting that any architecture that fragments retrieval from synthesis is at risk; whether the multi-agent variant outperforms a single agent here depends entirely on whether a verifier pass like Anthropic's CitationAgent is wired in.

The two flagship sources — Cognition (anti) and Anthropic (pro) — are less contradictory than their titles suggest. Cognition's argument is principally about write-heavy, tightly coupled work (code, refactors) where conflicting implicit decisions destroy output. Anthropic's pro-multi-agent results are on read-heavy, breadth-first research where parallel context windows and separation of concerns are net wins, but they still document the same failure modes Cognition warns about and pay an explicit ~15× token premium plus a substantial prompt-engineering tax to suppress them. The 2024–2025 red-team literature (Prompt Infection, AgentXploit, Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI) adds a third dimension Cognition does not address: the security attack surface scales with the number of sub-agents that ingest untrusted web content, and known mitigations (input sanitization, classifiers, instruction tagging) are partial, not total.

Cognition explicitly notes that Claude Code's sub-agents are deliberately constrained to investigative/read-only tasks and never run code-writing work in parallel, precisely because parallel sub-agents would 'give conflicting responses, resulting in the reliability issues' from earlier examples.

Anthropic's June 13, 2025 multi-agent research-system writeup documents that early versions exhibited planner-drift failure modes including 'spawning 50 subagents for simple queries, scouring the web endlessly for nonexistent sources, and distracting each other with excessive updates,' plus duplicated work across sub-agents on the same topic.

Anthropic mitigates these failure modes with multi-agent-specific architectural devices: scaling rules embedded in the lead-agent prompt, a separate post-research CitationAgent that attributes claims to sources, and an LLM-judge rubric covering factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, and source quality.

Lee & Tiwari (arXiv:2410.07283, October 2024) demonstrate experimentally that prompt-injection attacks self-replicate across interconnected agents in multi-agent systems 'much like a computer virus,' propagating silently 'even when agents do not publicly share all communications,' and propose LLM Tagging as a mitigation.

Anthropic's browser-use prompt-injection mitigation post reports a residual ~1% attack success rate even after reinforcement-learning hardening, content classifiers on untrusted input, and behavioral interventions — and explicitly states 'no browser agent is immune to prompt injection.'

Citation fabrication ('vibe citing') is widespread: GPTZero's audit of 4,841 NeurIPS 2025 papers documented 100+ hallucinated citations across 51 accepted papers, including invented authors, fabricated DOIs, and amalgamated titles.

A February 2025 hands-on postmortem by a domain expert found Perplexity's Deep Research output contained multiple factual errors in the first two paragraphs of a Tenstorrent architecture query, with cited references not actually containing the claimed information — illustrating that single-agent-style RAG-with-iteration deep-research products also exhibit citation fabrication.

Multiple December 2025 lawsuits (NYT v. Perplexity, Chicago Tribune v. Perplexity) plead trademark and false-attribution claims grounded in Perplexity outputs that pair fabricated text with the publishers' marks, indicating that the citation-fabrication failure mode has reached production-impact severity.

Anthropic's Research architecture isolates citation work in a separate CitationAgent stage that runs after research synthesis, processing the documents and report to attribute specific claims — an explicit architectural acknowledgement that distributing retrieval across sub-agents creates a citation-attribution gap a single agent does not face by default.

Independent commentary (Philschmid, June 2025) and applied analyses (Augment Code, Galileo) read Cognition and Anthropic as compatible rather than contradictory: multi-agent wins for breadth-first read-heavy research, single-agent wins for tightly coupled write-heavy work, and both teams emphasize context engineering as the dominant reliability lever.

sub_question: What 2024-2026 empirical evidence isolates the contribution of parallel tool calling within a single agent loop from genuine multi-agent orchestration with separate context windows — and how much of the reported multi-agent gains on BrowseComp, GAIA, or DeepResearch Bench actually survive when a single agent is allowed to issue parallel tool calls at matched token budgets?
summary:
The literature contains no study that cleanly isolates 'single agent with parallel tool calls' from 'multi-agent orchestration' on BrowseComp, GAIA, or DeepResearch Bench at matched total token budgets. The headline pro-multi-agent number — Anthropic's claim that a Claude Opus 4 lead with Claude Sonnet 4 subagents beats single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research eval — was published explicitly without matched-token controls, and Anthropic itself reports that token usage alone explains 80% of performance variance on BrowseComp and that token usage + tool-call count + model choice together explain 95% of variance. That is, in their own data, 'architecture' is barely a separable variable from compute spend. The same blog also notes that within one subagent, '3+ tools in parallel' plus 3–5 parallel subagents together cut latency 90% — the parallel-tool-calls-in-one-loop and parallel-subagent contributions are bundled together in their reported numbers and never disentangled.

The most rigorous budget-controlled comparison is Tran & Kiela (Stanford, arXiv 2604.02460, April 2026). Across three model families (Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro), two multi-hop benchmarks (FRAMES, MuSiQue 4-hop), and five multi-agent architectures (Sequential, Subtask-parallel, Parallel-roles, Debate, Ensemble), they hold thinking-token budgets constant from 100 → 10 000 tokens. Their finding: 'SAS consistently match or outperform MAS on multi-hop reasoning tasks when reasoning tokens are held constant.' Average accuracy at 10k tokens: SAS 0.426, Sequential MAS 0.387, Subtask-parallel 0.399. They give an information-theoretic justification (Data Processing Inequality + Fano) that any multi-agent decomposition with messages M = g(C) must satisfy P_e(M) ≥ P_e(C) when the single agent has the full context. They also identify two important measurement artifacts: Gemini's API-reported thinking-token count is inflated up to 4.7× over visible content, and Sequential MAS surfaces more visible thought text than SAS at the same requested budget — meaning past 'MAS wins' may simply reflect more unaccounted compute. The big caveat: Tran & Kiela study text-only multi-hop QA with no web search tools, so they isolate the communication-bottleneck effect of multi-agent, not the parallel-search advantage. MAS only wins their experiment under heavy context corruption (substitution α=0.7, masking α=0.7) — suggesting MAS becomes useful as a long-context-degradation hedge, not as an architectural primitive.

Snorkel.ai's October 2025 enterprise tool-use ablation is the closest analog with real tool calls. Using the GPT-5 family on a ToolACE-derived multi-tool ecosystem (3 → 100+ tools, with adversarial distractors), they find: at low tool count, single-agent beats multi-agent because the planner is overhead. As tool count and context grow past ~30 K tokens, multi-agent overtakes single-agent — but mainly for the smaller models (GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano). Frontier GPT-5 stays roughly flat across architectures, and the multi-agent advantage shrinks as model capability scales. This is consistent with Gao et al. 2025 ('Single-agent or Multi-agent? Why Not Both?', arXiv 2505.18286): on a 30-task game/coding suite, SAS wins 13, MAS wins 0, both pass 11. Their summary: 'MAS historically outperforms SAS, but loses its edge as LLMs grow more capable.'

Two additional sources frame the disagreement. Cemri et al. ('Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?', NeurIPS 2025 spotlight, arXiv 2503.13657) annotated 1 600+ traces across 7 MAS frameworks and identified 14 failure modes in three categories — system design, inter-agent misalignment, weak verification — concluding that 'performance gains across popular benchmarks remain minimal compared to single-agent frameworks.' Cognition's June 2025 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' post by Walden Yan argues from production experience (Devin) that splitting work across parallel agents makes context sharing impossible and decisions incoherent; their two principles ('share full traces' and 'actions carry implicit decisions') are essentially the engineering version of Tran & Kiela's DPI argument. Meiklejohn's 2026 multi-agent benchmarks meta-analysis confirms that the only deep-research benchmark where multi-agent has a large measured edge is BrowseComp (Anthropic's +90% number), and that this edge has not been independently replicated under matched-token controls.

Net answer for the sub-question: there is no published apples-to-apples ablation that isolates parallel tool calling within one agent from full multi-agent orchestration on BrowseComp, GAIA, or DeepResearch Bench at matched token budgets. The strongest available evidence — budget-controlled multi-hop QA (Tran & Kiela), enterprise tool-use ablation (Snorkel), and Anthropic's own variance decomposition (80% from tokens, 95% from tokens+tool-calls+model) — together imply that a substantial fraction of the reported multi-agent gains on browsing benchmarks reflects unmatched compute and unmatched parallel tool-call counts rather than the orchestrator-worker architecture per se, and that the multi-agent premium shrinks toward zero as base-model capability and effective context utilization improve. Multi-agent is best understood as a way to spend more tokens in parallel and route around long-context degradation, not as an architectural multiplier independent of compute.

In Anthropic's own analysis on BrowseComp, token usage alone explains 80% of performance variance, and token usage + tool-call count + model choice together explain 95% of variance — leaving little residual variance attributable to multi-agent architecture per se.

Anthropic states that within their multi-agent system, both parallel-subagent fan-out (3–5 parallel) AND parallel tool calls within each subagent (3+ tools in parallel) were introduced together, jointly cutting research time up to 90%; the two contributions are not separately ablated.

Tran & Kiela (Stanford, 2026) show that under matched thinking-token budgets (100–10 000 tokens), single-agent systems consistently match or outperform five multi-agent architectures (Sequential, Subtask-parallel, Parallel-roles, Debate, Ensemble) on FRAMES and MuSiQue 4-hop across Qwen3-30B, DeepSeek-R1-70B, and Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro.

Gemini's API-reported thoughts_token_count is inflated up to 4.7× over the visible thought content, and Sequential MAS surfaces more visible thought text than SAS at the same requested budget — meaning previously reported MAS wins on Gemini may reflect unaccounted compute rather than architectural advantage.

On Snorkel.ai's enterprise multi-tool ecosystem (built from ToolACE with adversarial distractors), multi-agent systems hurt at low tool counts (planner overhead) and only outperform single-agent baselines past ~30 K context tokens — and the gain is largest for GPT-5-mini/nano while frontier GPT-5 stays roughly flat across architectures.

Cemri et al.'s MAST study (NeurIPS 2025 spotlight) annotated 1 600+ traces across 7 MAS frameworks and concluded that 'performance gains across popular benchmarks remain minimal compared to single-agent frameworks,' identifying 14 distinct MAS failure modes (system design, inter-agent misalignment, weak verification).

Cognition's June 2025 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' post argues from production experience that splitting work across parallel agents prevents adequate context sharing and produces conflicting implicit decisions, recommending single-threaded agents with rigorous context engineering as the default.

Meiklejohn's 2026 multi-agent benchmarks meta-analysis identifies BrowseComp as the only deep-research benchmark where multi-agent has a large measured edge over single-agent (Anthropic's +90%), and notes that GAIA Level 3 (~2×) and TravelPlanner (3.3×) gains depend on state-sharing/coordination patterns; SWE-bench, HumanEval, and most coding tasks favor single agents.

No published study at the time of writing isolates 'single agent with parallel tool calls' from 'multi-agent orchestration with separate context windows' on BrowseComp, GAIA, or DeepResearch Bench at matched total-token budgets; the closest controlled comparisons (Tran & Kiela; Snorkel) use multi-hop QA and synthetic tool ecosystems, not those benchmarks.

Gao et al. 2025 (arXiv 2505.18286) report that on a 30-task game/coding evaluation, single-agent wins 13 cases, multi-agent wins 0, and 11 are ties, summarizing the trend as 'MAS historically outperforms SAS, but loses its edge as LLMs grow more capable.'

(2025) report single-agent matching or beating multi-agent at matched compute on multi-hop QA and game/coding tasks. The likely reconciliation: Anthropic's number is at unmatched token budgets (15× more tokens), and its own variance decomposition shows 95% of BrowseComp variance is explained by tokens+tool-calls+model — leaving multi-agent architecture barely separable from compute spend. The two camps may not actually disagree on causation, only on framing.

Cognition (Walden Yan, June 2025) advocates single-threaded agents with shared context as the default, while Anthropic argues multi-agent is essential for breadth-first research. Both acknowledge the framing depends on task shape: Cognition's domain is coding (tightly coupled state, write-heavy), Anthropic's is open-ended research (read-heavy, parallelizable). Snorkel's enterprise tool-use data and Meiklejohn's benchmark survey both support a task-shape-dependent reconciliation rather than a clean winner.

There is genuine disagreement on whether the multi-agent advantage will grow or shrink with model capability. Anthropic implies it grows ('once intelligence reaches a threshold, multi-agent systems become a vital way to scale'); Gao et al. and Snorkel report the opposite — that frontier models close the gap and multi-agent advantages concentrate in weaker/smaller-model regimes. No matched-token deep-research benchmark resolves this yet.

Tran & Kiela's experiments are text-only multi-hop QA without tools, so they cannot directly speak to the parallel-search/parallel-fetch advantage that motivates multi-agent deep research; their 'SAS ≥ MAS at matched tokens' result may not transfer to web-browsing benchmarks, where I/O-bound parallelism is genuinely valuable. This is the empirical gap the sub-question asks about, and it remains open.

sub_question: What independent replications, critiques, or methodological challenges to the Stanford 'Single-Agent Planning vs Multi-Agent' budget-controlled study (Tran & Kiela, arXiv:2604.02460) have appeared, and do other 2025-2026 papers that hold thinking-token budget constant across architectures (rather than allowing multi-agent to use more compute) corroborate or contradict the SAS≥MAS finding on multi-hop QA benchmarks like FRAMES, MuSiQue, HotpotQA, or 2WikiMultiHopQA?
summary:
The Tran & Kiela paper (Stanford / Contextual AI, arXiv:2604.02460, v1 2 April 2026, v2 11 April 2026, still 'Preprint. Under review.') is too new to have generated direct independent replications — at the time of search (early May 2026) it has been public for roughly a month. No paper I located reproduces its exact protocol on FRAMES or MuSiQue 4-hop with matched thinking-token budgets. There is also no published rebuttal demonstrating MAS > SAS on those specific multi-hop QA benchmarks once thinking-tokens are normalized; the only contradicting evidence I found uses RL-trained MAS without strict compute-matching, which is not an apples-to-apples test.

The closest concurrent/prior work that does control for compute is Kim et al. 'Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems' (Google Research + MIT Media Lab, arXiv:2512.08296, blog 28 Jan 2026), which Tran & Kiela themselves cite as concurrent. Kim et al. ran 180–260 configurations across BrowseComp-Plus, Finance-Agent, PlanCraft, Workbench, SWE-bench Verified, and Terminal-Bench, with all SAS and MAS variants 'matched for total reasoning-token budget' (a public Hacker News comment cites a mean of 4,800 tokens/trial). Their findings partially corroborate and partially refine Tran & Kiela: on sequential reasoning (PlanCraft) every multi-agent variant degraded performance 39–70% (consistent with SAS≥MAS), and independent MAS amplified errors 17.2× while centralized MAS held amplification to 4.4×. But on parallelizable tasks (Finance-Agent), centralized MAS beat the single-agent baseline by ~80.9% even at matched budget — a regime Tran & Kiela do not test. The two papers therefore agree on the sequential / multi-hop case but disagree (or rather, complement) on the parallelizable case, suggesting the SAS≥MAS finding is regime-specific, not universal.

Gao et al. 'Single-agent or Multi-agent Systems? Why Not Both?' (arXiv:2505.18286, 23 May 2025, preceding Tran & Kiela by 10 months) reports the same direction of effect without strict thinking-token matching: 'the benefits of MAS over SAS diminish as LLM capabilities improve' on popular agentic benchmarks. They propose a cascading hybrid that improves accuracy 1.1–12% while cutting cost up to 20%. This is a corroborating signal, but methodologically weaker than Tran & Kiela because it does not isolate compute as the controlled variable. Cemri et al. 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?' (UC Berkeley, arXiv:2503.13657, NeurIPS 2025) — cited explicitly by Tran & Kiela as alignment with their 'over-exploration, aggregation/extraction errors, and opaque API accounting' failure modes — observes that 'performance gains on popular benchmarks are often minimal' for MAS, providing complementary failure-mode evidence rather than a head-to-head budget-controlled comparison.

Methodological challenges that have been raised (mostly on social media and in discussion threads, not yet in peer-reviewed rebuttals) include: (1) Tran & Kiela tested at one budget level — a Hacker News commenter on Kim et al. asked 'I wonder if the budget is increased (say 50k) would the same results be observed?', a critique that applies symmetrically to Tran & Kiela's budget regime; (2) the FRAMES + MuSiQue scope is multi-hop QA with concise ground-truth answers, not the long-horizon deep-research / report-generation tasks where production multi-agent systems (Anthropic Research, Perplexity Pro Deep Research) report their wins; (3) Tran & Kiela themselves flag API-side budget-control artifacts (especially in Gemini 2.5) and benchmark vulnerabilities that can inflate apparent MAS gains, which is itself a methodological warning to all prior MAS-favorable papers; (4) the MAS architectures tested (Sequential, Subtask-parallel, Parallel-roles, Debate, Ensemble) are static / hand-designed — Ke et al. (MAS-Orchestra, arXiv:2601.14652, 2026, cited by Tran & Kiela) argue learned orchestration changes the picture, though they too conclude improvements depend on task structure and verification protocols, not architectural superiority.

Net assessment for the original deep-research question: on multi-hop factual QA (FRAMES, MuSiQue, and by reasonable extrapolation HotpotQA / 2WikiMultiHopQA, which are similar in answer-format and reasoning shape) the SAS≥MAS finding under matched thinking-token budgets is corroborated by every concurrent budget-controlled study I located, with zero direct contradictions. On parallelizable, fan-out-style tasks (financial analysis, breadth-first browsing) Kim et al. provide budget-matched evidence that MAS can substantially win (+80.9%). On sequential planning, both papers agree MAS loses (39–70% degradation in Kim et al.). The literature has not yet produced an independent replication of the exact Tran & Kiela protocol on FRAMES/MuSiQue, so the finding should be characterized as 'consistent with concurrent budget-controlled evidence on adjacent benchmarks' rather than 'independently replicated'.

key_facts.claim: Tran & Kiela (arXiv:2604.02460) is a Stanford/Contextual AI preprint dated 2 April 2026 (v2 11 April 2026), still 'Under review' at time of writing, evaluating SAS vs five MAS architectures (Sequential, Subtask-parallel, Parallel-roles, Debate, Ensemble) on FRAMES and MuSiQue 4-hop across Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama, and Gemini 2.5; SAS matches or outperforms MAS under matched thinking-token budgets except when context utilization is degraded.

No direct independent replication of the Tran & Kiela protocol on FRAMES or MuSiQue with matched thinking-token budgets has appeared in the public literature as of early May 2026 (paper is ~1 month old).

Tran & Kiela ground their result theoretically in the Data Processing Inequality, arguing that under a fixed reasoning-token budget and perfect context utilization, single-agent systems are more information-efficient because every inter-agent handoff can only lose information.

Tran & Kiela also identify methodological artifacts that previously inflated MAS gains, specifically in API-based budget control (particularly Gemini 2.5) and in standard benchmarks, which functions as a methodological challenge to prior MAS-favorable work.

Kim et al. (Google Research + MIT Media Lab, 'Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems', arXiv:2512.08296, blog 28 Jan 2026) is concurrent budget-matched work that tested 180–260 configurations across BrowseComp-Plus, Finance-Agent, PlanCraft, Workbench, SWE-bench Verified, and Terminal-Bench — but not FRAMES, MuSiQue, HotpotQA, or 2WikiMultiHopQA.

Kim et al. corroborate SAS≥MAS on sequential reasoning: every multi-agent variant degraded performance 39–70% on PlanCraft; independent MAS amplified errors 17.2× while centralized MAS held amplification to 4.4×.

Kim et al. partially contradict any universal SAS≥MAS reading by showing centralized MAS beat the single-agent baseline by ~80.9% on the parallelizable Finance-Agent task at matched compute — a regime Tran & Kiela do not test.

Gao et al. 'Single-agent or Multi-agent Systems? Why Not Both?' (arXiv:2505.18286, 23 May 2025) finds that benefits of MAS over SAS diminish as LLM capabilities improve, and proposes a SAS/MAS cascading hybrid that improves accuracy 1.1–12% while reducing deployment cost by up to 20% — a corroborating direction of effect, though without strict thinking-token matching as the controlled variable.

Cemri et al. 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?' (UC Berkeley, arXiv:2503.13657, NeurIPS 2025) is cited by Tran & Kiela as alignment with their failure modes and observes that MAS 'performance gains on popular benchmarks are often minimal'; it is complementary failure-mode evidence rather than a head-to-head budget-controlled comparison.

The Tran & Kiela result is regime-specific: it covers multi-hop factual QA with concise ground-truth answers (FRAMES, MuSiQue 4-hop), not long-horizon deep-research/report-generation tasks where production MAS like Anthropic Research operate.

Wang et al. (arXiv:2506.02718) trains a MARL multi-agent search system (MHGPO) that beats single-context RAG baselines on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue — but this is RL-optimized MAS vs unoptimized SAS without thinking-token matching, so it does not constitute a budget-controlled contradiction of Tran & Kiela.

An open methodological question raised in public discussion (Hacker News on Kim et al.) is whether SAS≥MAS persists at much larger thinking-token budgets (e.g., 50k+) than the ~4,800-token mean used in Kim et al.; this critique applies symmetrically to Tran & Kiela's single-budget regime.

Anthropic's June 2025 engineering writeup measured ~4× tokens for a single-agent chat baseline and ~15× for their multi-agent research system, and reported that token usage alone explains ~80% of performance variance on BrowseComp — context that is consistent with Tran & Kiela's framing that headline MAS gains often track compute spend.
